page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.e4.2xlarge is a memory-oriented shared virtual server instance powered by the KVM hypervisor. It is configured with 8 shared vCPUs derived from 4 physical cores on an Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.5 GHz with a 40 MB L3 cache. The instance features an x86_64 architecture supporting standard instruction set extensions including AVX, AES, BMI2, and FMA, but lacks modern AVX-512 and AMX instruction sets. Memory provision is high relative to processing resources, delivering 64.0 GB of system RAM at an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio. The configuration includes no local instance storage and provides a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps with no complimentary public IPv4 addresses and zero hardware GPU accelerators.

Performance testing indicates a divergence between single-threaded throughput and parallel multi-core capabilities. Single-core execution on the Broadwell-era Xeon E5-2682 v4 is constrained, with stress-ng single-core performance and single-threaded bzip3 decompression registering in the bottom 10 percent of evaluated systems. Conversely, parallel execution scales adequately across the 8 shared vCPUs, yielding average benchmark brackets for multi-core stress-ng at 7603.91 and a PassMark CPU score of 8524.6. Memory throughput demonstrates stable mid-tier bandwidth, delivering 48.82 GB/sec uncached reads and 33.48 GB/sec uncached writes. Evaluated application metrics reflect this profile, demonstrating moderate performance for Redis SET operations at 9.13 million operations per second and static web serving throughput at 8.41 GB/sec.

The instance architecture presents a distinct operational tradeoff centered on memory density versus computational overhead. Because CPU resources use a shared allocation model on legacy Intel hardware, compute-intensive execution, high-throughput cryptographic operations, and complex database workloads exhibit weaker benchmark profiles. However, the qualitative cost efficiency is favorable for memory-bound applications that require substantial address space without paying for dedicated high-frequency compute cores or bundled high-speed NVMe storage. Suitable workloads include medium-scale in-memory caching tiers such as Redis, internal static web servers, lightweight memory-heavy ETL preprocessing, and development or staging environments requiring ample memory capacity.
